map.alt: A hand-drawn contour map of the valley, its hills ringed with contour lines and its temples, huts and roads marked in ink.

epigraph.text: In its microcosm it is a replica of the entire universe... it could have been anywhere. But this valley lies forgotten to the outside world. Thus it is nowhere.

places.name: Fort Ruins
places.book: Built by the Maharaja of Kamboj in the era of the Mongol invasions and thought impregnable: five gates, an approach whose bends look like dead ends, a doorless royal gym attackers could enter only one at a time, and a math whose sage vanished when the fort fell.

real.name: Daulatabad (Devagiri) Fort
real.why: Deceptive gates and false doors built to confuse attackers, the labyrinthine Andheri passage, and layered walls with spiked gates. It fell to Khalji in 1296, the right era, and its saint-commander Janardan Swami has a samadhi in a cave inside it, a close echo of the fort's sage. Even the name echoes.
real.alsoFrom: Harihar Fort, Nashik - 117 rock-cut steps at 75-80 degrees, for the turret the soldiers had to climb

images.alt: The dark rock-cut entrance of the Andheri passage at Daulatabad, a single low doorway in a carved stone face.
images.commons: Andheri or Dark Passage located inside Daulatabad Fort or Deogiri Fort, Daulatabad, Maharashtra 01.jpg

images.alt: Near-vertical steps cut into the bare rock of Harihar fort, climbing out of shot.

places.name: The pushkarini below the fort
places.book: "A series of symmetric steps cascading inwards, much like an inverted temple vimana", with a square platform at the centre surrounded by water.

real.name: Stepped Tank, Royal Enclosure, Hampi
real.why: A five-tier symmetrical tank of chlorite schist whose steps form a pyramid on all four sides - the inverted vimana exactly. The central platform surrounded by water is the one part Hampi does not supply.
real.alsoFrom: Vandiyur Mariamman Teppakulam, Madurai - for the island platform

images.alt: The stepped tank at Hampi, tiers of dark stone steps descending on all four sides to green water.
A 19th-century photograph of the Teppakulam at Madurai: a broad temple tank with a pillared mandapam on an island at its centre.
images.commons: Vandiyur Mariamman Teppakulam bij Madurai, RP-F-00-5347-78.jpg

places.name: The chained stepwell
places.fiction: The stepwell of the tunnel mystery
places.book: At night, a stepwell whose short flight of steps leads to a vertical opening in the wall, covered by a metal frame chained from the far side.

real.name: Chand Baori, Abhaneri
real.why: The archetypal Indian stepwell - thirteen storeys, some 3,500 steps, an inverted pyramid - with gallery openings in its walls, standing beside the Harshat Mata temple. The chained opening itself is generic, so any gated stepwell would fit.

images.alt: The inverted pyramid of Chand Baori, thousands of narrow steps zig-zagging down three walls to the water.

places.name: The Bhoodara caves
places.fiction: The cave labyrinth under the valley
places.book: "A veritable chakravyuha inside the belly of the earth" - nobody who goes in is known to have come out - with mesolithic red-and-green paintings of hunting and foraging deep inside.

real.name: Bhimbetka's paintings in a Belum-like labyrinth
real.pin: Bhimbetka's paintings in a Belum-like labyrinth
real.why: A composite. Bhimbetka holds the earliest art in South Asia, Mesolithic hunting scenes painted mostly in red and white and occasionally in green. Belum supplies the maze: India's second-longest cave system, 3.2 km of passages mapped as a chakravyuha.
real.alsoFrom: Belum Caves, Nandyal - for the labyrinth

images.alt: Faded red figures of animals and hunters painted on the curved rock of a shelter wall at Bhimbetka.
A lit passage inside the Belum caves, the limestone glowing orange where the lamps catch it.
images.commons: The Main Caves, Belum, Andhra Pradesh.jpg

places.name: Bhoothnath Temple
places.fiction: The Kaal Bhairava temple, on Bhootnath taal
places.book: North-west of the valley at the foot of the forested Naga hill, "the only work in the valley made of soft stones... which lend well to carving", appearing to float on a natural lake. The seat of the aghori Keshav Bharan.

real.name: Kal Bhairav, Ujjain, in Halebidu's stone
real.why: Another composite. Ujjain's Kal Bhairav is chief of the eight Bhairavas, tied to the Kapalika and Aghora sects, with liquor still offered as one of the panchamakara - the left path the tantric baba teaches. Halebidu supplies the stone: soft chloritic schist, beside a lake.
real.alsoFrom: Hoysaleswara Temple, Halebidu - for the soft carved stone beside a lake

images.alt: The gateway of the Kal Bhairav temple at Ujjain, whitewashed and painted, with worshippers in the arch.
The Hoysaleswara temple at Halebidu, its low soapstone walls carved in bands from plinth to eaves.

places.name: Mahavidya Temples
places.fiction: The temples of the ten Mahavidyas
places.book: A close-knit group of temples in a thicket where the mountain's boulders meet the plains: plain outside, richly adorned within, with a Sri Chakra yantra and a panel of the ten Mahavidyas, revered by a small Shakta community.

real.name: Kamakhya, on Nilachal hill
real.why: The main temple complex of the ten Mahavidyas, each with its own shrine grouped around the central temple, and regarded as the birthplace of Shakta tantrism. The book's secondary character is even named Kamakhya.

images.alt: The Kamakhya temple's beehive dome above its plastered walls, red pennants flying from the shrines around it.

places.name: Sri Mukteshwar temple
places.fiction: The Mahant's seat, the centre of culture in the valley
places.book: Headed for generations by the Mahant's family of pujaris. Its amalaka and kalasha, atop the vimana, are visible from every part of the village.

real.name: Mukteshvara Temple, Bhubaneswar
real.why: The same name. A 10th-century Kalinga-style Shiva temple whose curved tower is crowned by an amalaka and kalasha, and a landmark of Odishan temple architecture.

images.alt: The Mukteshvara temple at Bhubaneswar, its carved sandstone tower rising behind the arched torana at its gate.

places.name: Gaumukh Hill and the Ram temples
places.fiction: The langoors' hill, with its hilltop Hanuman shrine
places.book: Gaumukh hill, "the home of langoors", carries a Hanuman shrine on top and Ram temples along its base. On the trek it appears as a muddy lotus pushkarini beside a small white Hanuman mandir, grey langurs in the trees.

real.name: Anjanadri hill, Anegundi
real.why: Revered as Hanuman's birthplace: a white hilltop temple reached by some 575 steps, monkeys everywhere, and Rama and Sita shrines below - which is the Ram temples along the base as well.

images.alt: The small whitewashed Hanuman temple on top of Anjanadri hill, an orange flag streaming from its spire above the valley.

places.name: Kamal Taal
places.fiction: The lotus lake beside Gaumukh hill
places.book: The lake beside the hill; the name is simply "lotus lake".

real.name: Pampa Sarovar
real.why: A sacred lotus-filled pond of the Ramayana, directly below Anjanadri - the same pairing of hill and water the map has.

images.alt: Pampa Sarovar seen from the hill above: a rectangular green tank fringed by palms, with boulder country beyond.

places.name: Naga Forest and Nagadwara Hill
places.fiction: The realm of the Nagas, who worship Dhumavati
places.book: The most ardent tantrics gather around the Bhootnath temple at the foot of Nagadwara hill, and the forest beyond is "the realm of the Nagas who worship Dhumavati".

real.name: Nagdwari, Pachmarhi
real.why: A complex of naga cave shrines deep in forest and cliffs, reached by a hard three-day pilgrimage at Nag Panchami. The name matches almost exactly. The Dhumavati connection is the book's own.
real.noPhoto: No freely licensed photograph of Nagdwari could be credited honestly - the one file on Commons names its uploader as "Don't Know". The shrines are photographed mostly during the pilgrimage itself.

places.name: The ancient temple of the forest
places.fiction: Where the Kaula rites are held
places.book: The site of the Kaula left-path rites, the panchamakara, whose aftermath Dvij links to his kundalini rising to svadhishthana.

real.name: Chausath Yogini temple, Hirapur
real.why: A hypaethral - roofless - circular shrine of the Kaula and Kapalika sects, forgotten until it was rediscovered in 1953. Mitaoli and Bhedaghat are the same form in remoter settings.
real.alsoFrom: Chausath Yogini, Mitaoli and Bhedaghat - the same circle, remoter

images.alt: The low circular outer wall of the Chausath Yogini temple at Hirapur, open to the sky.
The circular Chausath Yogini temple at Mitaoli, a ring of pillared cells around an open court on a hilltop.
images.commons: 0121621 Chausath Yogini and Shiva Temple, Mitaoli Madhya Pradesh.jpg

places.name: Vidgati's shrine and the cave settlement
places.fiction: The Charvaka semi-saint's shrine, half way up Dronagiri
places.book: A plateau flattened centuries ago by a vanished Buddhist settlement, caves along the ridge used as dwellings, the largest probably a monastery with ruined chaityas, a rock-cut Harihara "maybe 12th century", and Jain monks once living there.

real.name: Badami's Harihara and Jain cave, on an Ellora-like ridge
real.pin: Badami's Harihara and Jain cave, on an Ellora-like ridge
real.why: Badami holds some of India's earliest Harihara reliefs, in caves 1 and 3, next door to a Jain cave. Ellora supplies the rest: Buddhist, Hindu and Jain caves side by side along one escarpment, with monasteries and chaitya halls. The Charvaka shrine itself has no counterpart - Charvaka left almost no sites, which is the book's point.
real.alsoFrom: Ellora - for the Buddhist settlement along the ridge

images.alt: The Harihara relief in Badami cave 3, one figure whose left half is Shiva and right half Vishnu, carved in red sandstone.
The pillared entrance of the Jain cave at Badami, cave 4, cut into the cliff face.
images.commons: 7th to 8th century Digambara Jain cave entrance, Badami cave 4, Karnataka.jpg

images.alt: A 19th-century photograph of the Vishvakarma chaitya at Ellora, its carved gallery and arched window above the entrance.
images.commons: Exterior of Sootar Ki Jhonpri, Ellora.jpg

places.name: The dolmen in the field of fireflies
places.fiction: Where the party shelters on the anahata night
places.book: The party shelters under an ancient dolmen in a large open field.

real.name: Hire Benakal, Koppal
real.why: India's largest megalithic necropolis - some 400 monuments, many of them dolmens, dated 800-200 BCE - and on UNESCO's tentative list.

images.alt: Dolmens standing among boulders on the hillside at Hire Benakal, their capstones tilted, under a grey sky.

places.name: The Vedic ashram of Kritya Rishi
places.fiction: Near the top of Dronagiri, where the rites are still done faithfully
places.book: The round-nosed man identifies Bhavi's diagram as a Vedic altar of homa-kundas, and mentions bird-shaped altars.

real.name: The Agnicayana at Panjal
real.why: The 1975 Athirathram at Panjal, documented by Frits Staal, is the most famous living example of the altar geometry the book describes: a twelve-day rite built around a falcon-shaped altar of thousands of bricks. This pairs the ritual, not the Himalayan setting.

images.alt: A replica of the falcon-shaped citi laid out in terracotta bricks, with the ritual vessels and implements arranged beside it.

places.name: Mount Dronagiri
places.fiction: The tallest peak around the valley, where the plant is found
places.book: The trek up it is the second half of the story.

real.name: Dunagiri, Chamoli
real.why: Named directly. By legend the mountain Hanuman carried off for the Sanjeevani herb - and the villagers there famously do not worship Hanuman, for breaking their deity, which sits oddly and well against the book's Hanuman shrines lower down.

images.alt: The snow summit of Dunagiri seen from Kuari Pass at dawn, pink light on the ridge above dark forested slopes.

places.name: The valley of white flowers
places.fiction: Where Dvij walks alone in the Epilogue
places.book: Dvij walks alone "through the valley of the white flowers that seemed to be reaching out into nothingness".

real.name: Valley of Flowers National Park
real.why: In the same district as Dunagiri, and in some traditions identified with the mountain of herbs itself. A fitting last real place for the last page.

images.alt: The Valley of Flowers in bloom, a meadow of small flowers running up to steep green mountainsides and cloud.
images.artist: Original: Rohit Sharma Derivative work: UnpetitproleX
images.commons: Valley of flowers national park, Uttarakhand, India 03 (edit).jpg

places.name: Sheetal Lake
places.fiction: Fed by the Vaitarna, its water once said to cure illness
places.book: Dvij explains the cure with the bacteriophage research on the Ganga.

real.name: The Ganga, and what was found in its water
real.why: The antibacterial power of Ganga water, first reported by Ernest Hankin in the 1890s and later explained by bacteriophages, is real history and is exactly the move Dvij makes. The Vaitarna is a real river in Maharashtra and, in myth, the river the dead cross - a name, and nothing more.
real.alsoFrom: The Vaitarna, Maharashtra - the name only

images.alt: The ghats of Varanasi seen from the Ganga, stone steps and temple buildings rising from the water with boats moored below.
An electron micrograph of a T2 bacteriophage, its angular head and tail fibres in grey against the stain.
images.commons: Enterobacteria phage T2 transmission electron micrograph.jpg

images.alt: The Vaitarna river in Palghar, brown water between wooded banks.

fictional.name: Professor's Lodge
fictional.note: At most a colonial-era forest rest house as a type, rather than a building.

fictional.name: Forest Officer's Bungalow
fictional.note: At most a colonial-era forest rest house as a type, rather than a building.

fictional.name: Madangi Van
fictional.note: Where the Somasuras dwell. Best left fictional.
